question: An article on the conditions for authorisation of a ‘primatology centre’ has incidentally revealed that the majority of primates used for biomedical experiments in France still come from abroad1. However, according to Articles 9 and 10 of Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes, animals taken from the wild should not be used in these procedures if it can be avoided.

In the question for written answer E-001141/20222, I informed the Commission that Article 10 of the aforementioned directive required them to publish a study, by 10 November 2022 at the latest, on the feasibility of laboratories being supplied exclusively with non-human primates bred on farms. 1.
Can the Commission tell us whether it has finally carried out this study and, if so, what are its findings?
The Commission also stated that it intended to prohibit the use of non-human primates in scientific procedures3. Has there finally been progress in this direction?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2024) The study on the feasibility of sourcing non-human primates only from self-sustaining colonies was published1 as required in Article 10(2) of Directive 2010/63/EU2. The study concluded that it was not possible to determine whether the aspiration of sourcing non-human primates only from self-sustaining colonies will be achievable in the near future.

It seemed possible that squirrel monkeys, prosimians, marmosets, and vervets may continue to be supplied entirely from self-sustaining colonies, however, the evidence presented suggested that for cynomolgus macaques, there was no realistic possibility of sourcing only from selfsustaining colonies in the short or medium term.

As macaques and vervets are mostly sourced from overseas, and there are no EU drivers to these breeders to supply from self-sustaining colonies other than customer request and preference, users in the EU may be unable to obtain animals from self-sustaining colonies.

As the Commission noted in its reply to written question E-1141/2022, to which the Honourable Member refers, the Directive prohibits the use of wild-caught non-human primates in scientific procedures. It is not meant and does not prohibit the use of non-human primates.

According to the Animal Use Reporting EU System (ALURES) statistical EU database3, no wild-caught non-human primates have been used in the EU since 2016. This prohibition has now been followed by an obligation to only use non-human primates whose parents have been bred in captivity. This obligation took effect in November 2022.
Competent authorities may grant exemptions from this obligation on the basis of scientific justification.
1 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/chemicals/animals-science_en#implementation 2 Directive 2010/63/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 September 2010 on the protection
of animals used for scientific purposes, OJ L 276, 20.10.2010, p. 33–79. 3 https://webgate.ec.europa.eu/envdataportal/content/alures/section1_number-of-animals.html
